- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.7) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is strongly bearish (≤0.3) or shows sharp declines, model often underestimates; adjust upward to reflect mean reversion or rebound potential.
- Model frequently overreacts to recent spikes (e.g., +2–3% in 1–2 days), leading to over-forecasted peaks; apply lagged smoothing or dampen momentum-driven forecasts.
- In periods with high sentiment volatility (alternating 0.6–0.8), model tends to misalign with true trend; prioritize recent 7–14 day moving average over 30-day forecast.
- If sentiment history shows sustained bullishness with no reversal, model often fails to anticipate mean reversion; apply downward bias after 3–5 consecutive bullish sentiment days.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.3–0.6), model often underperforms; increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% to account for latent market momentum.
- Avoid forecasting sharp downward moves unless sentiment is consistently bearish (≤0.2) over 3+ days; otherwise, model tends to underestimate true drop magnitude.
